# Data Foundations {#sec-appdx-data-foundations dropcap="chapter-opening"}

Data problems rarely present as data problems. They surface as a training run that will not speed up, an accelerator sitting idle, accuracy eroding while dashboards stay green, or an evaluation whose verdict does not survive a second test set. The chapters use the back-of-the-envelope calculations and statistical tools that trace such symptoms back to measurable quantities without deriving them. This appendix supplies the derivations: transfer times, decode and storage-layout costs, tail probabilities, the sample sizes that make a measured rate trustworthy, and drift divergences. The tools lean on basic probability and on the data term of the iron law.

## How to Use This Appendix {.unnumbered}

This appendix is a reference organized by symptom. Each section states its tool compactly and points to the chapter that teaches the concept and applies it to a lighthouse workload, and @tbl-appdx-data-lookup maps each symptom to the section that carries the tool.

| **When the need is…**                                      | **Tool**                                       | **Section**                                                       |
|:-----------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Moving a dataset between sites or regions**              | Transfer time $\DataVolume/\Bandwidth$         | @sec-appdx-data-foundations-napkin-math-physics-data-gravity-9ae0 |
| **An accelerator starving behind CPU decode**              | Decode throughput by format                    | @sec-appdx-data-foundations-cost-serialization-b921               |
| **Reading a few features from wide records**               | Row versus columnar layout                     | @sec-appdx-data-foundations-row-vs-columnar-formats-bca2          |
| **A feature pipeline whose cost explodes**                 | Selection, projection, and join costs          | @sec-appdx-data-foundations-algebra-data-9792                     |
| **An average that looks fine while users complain**        | Session-level tail probability                 | @sec-appdx-data-foundations-distributions-long-tail-901f          |
| **Deciding whether a measured rate or difference is real** | Confidence interval, sample size, McNemar, A/B | @sec-appdx-data-foundations-sampling-estimation-5b1e              |
| **Accuracy drifting silently in production**               | KL divergence, PSI, KS statistic               | @sec-appdx-data-foundations-measuring-drift-divergence-a6dd       |
| **More data that no longer improves the model**            | Entropy and signal per byte                    | @sec-appdx-data-foundations-information-theory-systems-c033       |

: **Symptom-to-Section Lookup**: Each row pairs a symptom a chapter may name with the tool in this appendix that turns it into a measurement. {#tbl-appdx-data-lookup tbl-colwidths="[38,30,32]"}

```{python}
#| echo: false
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DATA GRAVITY TRANSFER TIMES
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-data-gravity—why we ship compute to data
# │
# │ Goal:    Compute transfer times for 1 TB/100 TB/1 PB at three bandwidths
# │          and an illustrative truck-transfer elapsed time.
# │ Show:    Human-readable durations (Seconds, Minutes, Hours, Days, Months).
# │ How:     T = Volume/Bandwidth, formatted via helper.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import (
    TB,
    PB,
    Gbps,
    second,
    minute,
    hour,
    day,
    DAYS_PER_MONTH,
)
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_count, fmt_time
from mlsysim import Systems  # Ethernet fabric bandwidths

class DataGravity:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────
    vol_1tb = 1 * TB  # scenario assumption: 1 TB dataset
    vol_100tb = 100 * TB  # scenario assumption: 100 TB dataset
    vol_1pb = 1 * PB  # scenario assumption: 1 PB dataset
    bw_1g = 1 * Gbps  # scenario assumption: 1 Gbps WAN link
    bw_10g = Systems.Fabrics.Ethernet_10G.bandwidth
    bw_100g = Systems.Fabrics.Ethernet_100G.bandwidth
    truck_load_time = 8 * hour  # scenario assumption: truck load time
    truck_transit_time = 32 * hour  # scenario assumption: truck transit time
    truck_unload_time = 8 * hour  # scenario assumption: truck unload time

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────
    t_1tb_1g = vol_1tb / bw_1g
    t_1tb_10g = vol_1tb / bw_10g
    t_1tb_100g = vol_1tb / bw_100g
    t_100tb_1g = vol_100tb / bw_1g
    t_100tb_10g = vol_100tb / bw_10g
    t_100tb_100g = vol_100tb / bw_100g
    t_1pb_1g = vol_1pb / bw_1g
    t_1pb_10g = vol_1pb / bw_10g
    t_1pb_100g = vol_1pb / bw_100g
    truck_total_time = truck_load_time + truck_transit_time + truck_unload_time

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_1tb_1g.to(second).magnitude - 8_000.0) < 1e-6, "1 TB at 1 Gbps should take 8,000 seconds")
    check(truck_total_time == 48 * hour, "Truck transfer example should total two days")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────
    t_1tb_1g_str = fmt_time(t_1tb_1g, hour, precision=1, commas=False, style="word")
    t_1tb_10g_str = fmt_time(t_1tb_10g, minute, precision=1, commas=False, style="word")
    t_1tb_100g_str = fmt_time(round(t_1tb_100g.to(second)), second, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    t_100tb_1g_str = fmt_time(round(t_100tb_1g.to(day)), day, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    t_100tb_10g_str = fmt_time(t_100tb_10g, hour, precision=1, commas=False, style="word")
    t_100tb_100g_str = fmt_time(t_100tb_100g, hour, precision=1, commas=False, style="word")
    t_1pb_1g_str = fmt_count(round(t_1pb_1g.to(day).magnitude / DAYS_PER_MONTH), commas=False, label="month")
    t_1pb_10g_str = fmt_time(round(t_1pb_10g.to(day)), day, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    t_1pb_100g_str = fmt_time(t_1pb_100g, hour, precision=1, commas=False, style="word")
    truck_1pb_str = fmt_time(truck_total_time, day, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
```

The first half of the appendix, Moving and Storing Data, serves the data pipelines in @sec-data-engineering-data-pipeline-architecture-b527. The second half, Probability and Statistics, provides the tests that decide whether a measured number can be trusted for the evaluations in @sec-benchmarking-statistical-methodological-issues-7aa5 and the operational monitoring in @sec-ml-operations-model-infrastructure-monitoring-3988.

## Moving and Storing Data {#sec-appdx-data-foundations-data-engineering-foundations-0c20}

Before a model can learn from a record, the record must leave storage, cross a network, and be decoded into tensors, and any one of those steps can idle an accelerator before a single gradient is computed. @Sec-data-engineering develops these stages inside a working pipeline; the reference models and tables below provide the templates for checking each cost by hand.

### Data gravity {#sec-appdx-data-foundations-napkin-math-physics-data-gravity-9ae0}

Copying a petabyte of training data across a 1 Gbps wide-area link takes months, whereas shipping the job to the cluster that already holds the data takes minutes. Data gravity[^fn-data-gravity-anchor] names this constraint, which transfer-time arithmetic makes precise, and @sec-data-engineering-data-gravity-adcb applies it to petabyte-scale training data. Network bandwidth is finite and does not grow with compute, so moving a large dataset can cost more time and energy than moving computation to where the data already lives.

[^fn-data-gravity-anchor]: **Data gravity**\index{Data gravity!appendix refresher}: Coined by Dave McCrory\index{McCrory, Dave|seealso{Data gravity}} in 2010 to describe how large datasets attract services and applications toward them, much as massive bodies attract smaller ones in physics [@mccrory2010datagravity].

The ideal line-rate transfer time is $\DatasetTransferTime= \DataVolume/\Bandwidth$ after converting data volume and bandwidth to compatible units (the calculations below convert decimal bytes and bits per second explicitly). For the large volumes here, latency is negligible. @Sec-appdx-machine-foundations-bandwidth-vs-latency-5320 gives the full equation with its latency term. @Tbl-data-gravity gives lower bounds; protocol overhead and endpoint limits increase them.

| **Data Volume** |       **1 Gbps (Standard WAN)**       |       **10 Gbps (High-End WAN)**       |      **100 Gbps (Direct Connect)**      |       **Truck (Illustrative)**       |
|:----------------|:-------------------------------------:|:--------------------------------------:|:---------------------------------------:|:------------------------------------:|
| **1 TB**        |  `{python} DataGravity.t_1tb_1g_str`  |  `{python} DataGravity.t_1tb_10g_str`  |  `{python} DataGravity.t_1tb_100g_str`  |                 N/A                  |
| **100 TB**      | `{python} DataGravity.t_100tb_1g_str` | `{python} DataGravity.t_100tb_10g_str` | `{python} DataGravity.t_100tb_100g_str` |                 N/A                  |
| **1 PB**        |  `{python} DataGravity.t_1pb_1g_str`  |  `{python} DataGravity.t_1pb_10g_str`  |  `{python} DataGravity.t_1pb_100g_str`  | `{python} DataGravity.truck_1pb_str` |

: **The Cost of Inertia**: These transfer times explain why we often "ship compute to data" rather than "ship data to compute." Network columns are lower bounds at sustained line rate. The truck entry is an illustrative elapsed-time model for 1 PB: 8 hours to load, 32 hours in transit, and 8 hours to unload, excluding scheduling and provisioning overhead. {#tbl-data-gravity tbl-colwidths="[23,20,20,20,17]"}

### Serialization cost {#sec-appdx-data-foundations-cost-serialization-b921}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: serialization-cost
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SERIALIZATION FORMAT PERFORMANCE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-serialization-cost—CPU decode overhead by format
# │
# │ Goal:    Show throughput and CPU cost for CSV, Protobuf, and Parquet.
# │ Show:    MB/s and cycles-per-value for each format.
# │ How:     Illustrative values, not portable benchmark results.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import MB, second
from mlsysim.fmt import MarkdownStr, check, fmt_bandwidth

class SerializationCost:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────
    csv_speed = 100 * (MB / second)
    parquet_speed = 1000 * (MB / second)
    csv_cycles = 100
    parquet_cycles = 10
    proto_speed = 300 * (MB / second)
    proto_cycles = 50

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────
    speedup = (parquet_speed / csv_speed).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────
    check(speedup == 10.0, f"Expected 10x speedup for Parquet over CSV, got {speedup}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────
    # Categorical labels are non-numeric table values.
    csv_speed_mb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(csv_speed, unit=MB / second, precision=0, commas=False, approx=True)
    parquet_speed_mb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(parquet_speed, unit=MB / second, precision=0, commas=True, approx=True)
    csv_cycles_str = MarkdownStr("High")
    parquet_cycles_str = MarkdownStr("Low")
    proto_speed_mb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(proto_speed, unit=MB / second, precision=0, commas=False, approx=True)
    proto_cycles_str = MarkdownStr("Medium")
```

Even after data arrives at the machine, it must be decoded before the accelerator can use it.[^fn-serialization-binary-format] The CPU cost of that decoding can differ by an order of magnitude across formats (@tbl-serialization-cost). Parsing text-based formats like JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) or CSV into floating-point numbers is CPU-bound and often leaves the accelerator idle.

[^fn-serialization-binary-format]: **Serialization**\index{Serialization!definition}: From Latin *serialis* (forming a series). The process of converting in-memory data structures into a byte stream for storage or transmission, and the reverse (*deserialization*). In ML pipelines, the choice of serialization format can dominate end-to-end training time; @sec-data-engineering-data-ingestion-8efc covers pipeline design strategies that minimize this overhead.

| **Format**   |                **Decoding Speed (MB/s)**                |           **Relative CPU Decode Cost**          | **Suitability**        |
|:-------------|:-------------------------------------------------------:|:-----------------------------------------------:|:-----------------------|
| **CSV/JSON** |   `{python} SerializationCost.csv_speed_mb_per_s_str`   |   `{python} SerializationCost.csv_cycles_str`   | Inspection/interchange |
| **Protobuf** |  `{python} SerializationCost.proto_speed_mb_per_s_str`  |  `{python} SerializationCost.proto_cycles_str`  | RPC/Messages           |
| **Parquet**  | `{python} SerializationCost.parquet_speed_mb_per_s_str` | `{python} SerializationCost.parquet_cycles_str` | Columnar storage       |

: **Serialization Overhead**: These illustrative values show why binary columnar formats can outperform row-based text, but they are not portable benchmarks. Arrow is an in-memory/IPC format; Parquet is a compressed storage format. {#tbl-serialization-cost tbl-colwidths="[21,27,27,25]"}

### Row and columnar formats {#sec-appdx-data-foundations-row-vs-columnar-formats-bca2}

Decoding speed per byte is only half of the format cost, because the storage layout also decides how many bytes a query must read from disk in the first place. Row-oriented formats such as CSV and JSON store data record-by-record, so reading the `age` field still requires parsing every attribute in each row, a layout that suits append-only logs while penalizing feature filtering. In contrast, Parquet stores compressed column chunks on disk, and Arrow provides a contiguous columnar representation in memory and across inter-process communication (IPC). Parquet readers can use *projection pushdown*\index{Projection pushdown} to fetch only the requested column chunks, while both formats feed *vectorized processing*\index{Vectorization!columnar processing}. Where the row layout forces a wide scan across all fields (`ID`, `Age`, `Loc`), the columnar layout isolates the target `Age` chunk and avoids moving irrelevant attributes (@fig-row-vs-col). @Sec-data-engineering-formats-compression-partitioning-8b17 develops format choice as a lever on the data term of the iron law.

::: {#fig-row-vs-col fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Storage Layouts**: Row-oriented formats group values by record, so the illustrated scan reads every field. Column-oriented formats group values by feature, so the illustrated scan reads only Age." fig-alt="Diagram contrasting row and column stores. The row store groups ID, Age, and Loc values by record and reads every column. The column store groups values by column and reads only Age."}

::: {#psp-appendix-data-accelerator-starvation-problem .callout-perspective title="The accelerator starvation problem"}

The choice of file format often determines whether a training pipeline is I/O bound or compute bound. Row-oriented formats force full-record scans, so storage layout compounds the decode cost whenever models consume a subset of tabular features, and the data-movement term of the iron law can silently become the critical path. @Sec-data-engineering-feeding-problem develops that starvation condition and the stage that binds it.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: data-algebra
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DATA ALGEBRA COST EXAMPLES
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-appdx-data-foundations-algebra-data-9792—projection waste, join cost
# │
# │ Goal:    Quantify the I/O waste of row-format projection and join cost.
# │ Show:    Waste percentage and network traffic for joins.
# │ How:     Scalar arithmetic from row/column sizes.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import KB, TB, byte, BYTES_INT32
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, check, fmt_percent, MarkdownStr, fmt_memory

class DataAlgebra:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────
    row_size_q = 1 * KB  # scenario assumption
    int_size_bytes = BYTES_INT32.to(byte).magnitude
    join_table_q = 1 * TB  # scenario assumption

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────
    waste_pct = (1 - (BYTES_INT32 / row_size_q).to("").magnitude) * 100
    join_network_q = 2 * join_table_q

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────
    check(waste_pct > 99, "Row-format waste should be >99%")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────
    row_size_kb_str = fmt_memory(row_size_q, unit=KB, precision=0, commas=False)
    int_size_bytes_value_str = fmt(int_size_bytes, precision=0, commas=False)
    waste_pct_str = fmt_percent(waste_pct / 100, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    join_table_tb_str = fmt_memory(join_table_q, unit=TB, precision=0, commas=False)
    join_network_tb_str = fmt_memory(join_network_q, unit=TB, precision=0, commas=False, approx=True)
```

### The algebra of data {#sec-appdx-data-foundations-algebra-data-9792}

Layout fixes what a scan can skip. The operations a feature pipeline applies decide how much it must read. Feature engineering turns raw records into the columns a model can learn from. A pipeline first narrows the population, then chooses the features, then attaches context from other tables. Those three moves correspond to three Structured Query Language (SQL)\index{Structured query language!feature pipeline primitives}\index{SQL!feature pipeline primitives} primitives, and their computational cost determines whether the feature job stays local, scans unnecessary bytes, or turns into a network shuffle.

1.  **Selection ($\RelationalSelection$)**: Filtering rows (for example, `WHERE age > 30`).
    *   **Cost**: For a table of $\TableRowCount$ rows, $\mathcal{O}(\log \TableRowCount+ \MatchingRowCount)$ if a B-tree index lookup returns $\MatchingRowCount$ rows; $\mathcal{O}(\TableRowCount)$ for a full scan.
2.  **Projection ($\pi$)**: Selecting columns (for example, `SELECT age`).
    *   **Cost**: Selected chunks plus decoding and metadata in columnar formats. This row-format example reads `{python} DataAlgebra.row_size_kb_str` for a `{python} DataAlgebra.int_size_bytes_value_str`-byte integer, wasting `{python} DataAlgebra.waste_pct_str` of the read.
3.  **Join ($\bowtie$)**: Combining tables. Usually the most expensive operation.
    *   **Shuffle Join**: Both tables are partitioned by key and exchanged over the network.
        *   **Cost**: Reshuffling both `{python} DataAlgebra.join_table_tb_str` tables moves `{python} DataAlgebra.join_network_tb_str`; partitioning and locality can reduce this.
    *   **Broadcast Join**: One small table is sent to all workers.
        *   **Cost**: $\BroadcastTableSize(\WorkerCount-1)$ bytes; the $\BroadcastTableSize$-byte table must fit on each of $\WorkerCount$ workers.

@Sec-data-engineering-scaling-distributed-processing-cb9b shows when these costs push feature processing beyond one machine. Formats, serialization, and algebraic primitives determine how efficiently data moves. They say nothing about whether the numbers computed from that data can be trusted, or whether the data has changed character since training. Answering those questions requires probability and statistics.

## Probability and Statistics {#sec-appdx-data-foundations-probability-statistics-3934}

Once records arrive at the model, summary averages can still mislead an engineer about whether a measured number can be trusted or whether the data has changed character since training: a low mean latency can hide frequent slow user sessions, a 0.5-point accuracy gain on a finite validation set can sit inside binomial noise, and a feature's mean can stay constant while its tails drift enough to degrade predictions. Four statistical tools separate those real effects from noise: tail probabilities for multi-request sessions, confidence intervals and paired or online sample-size formulas for finite evaluations, divergence measures for distribution shift, and information-theoretic units for the signal a dataset carries.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: long-tail-stats
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LONG-TAIL SCALE IMPACT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-appdx-data-foundations-distributions-long-tail-901f—P99 at scale
# │
# │ Goal:    Show how many users hit the P99 tail at production scale.
# │ Show:    1% of 1M users = 10,000 affected users.
# │ How:     Scalar multiplication.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_count, check

class LongTailScale:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────
    n_users = MILLION
    p99_ratio = 0.01

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────
    n_unhappy = n_users * p99_ratio

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────
    check(n_unhappy == 10_000, f"Expected 10,000 affected users, got {n_unhappy}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────
    n_users_str = fmt_count(n_users, scale="M", commas=False)
    n_unhappy_str = fmt_count(n_unhappy, label="user")
```

### Distributions and the long tail {#sec-appdx-data-foundations-distributions-long-tail-901f}

A service whose "p99" (99th percentile) latency is 500 ms leaves at most 1 percent of individual requests slower than 500 ms, yet at scale (`{python} LongTailScale.n_users_str` users) even a 1 percent affected-user rate degrades the experience of `{python} LongTailScale.n_unhappy_str`, and multi-request sessions push the fraction of users who see at least one slow response much higher. Because latency distributions are long-tailed\index{Tail latency!appendix refresher}, user-visible services are governed by high-percentile behavior rather than by the mean response time [@dean2013].

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tail-latency-probability
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TAIL-LATENCY SESSION PROBABILITY
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Callout "The Median Experience"
# │
# │ Goal:    Compute probability of at least one P99 spike in a user session.
# │ Show:    Formatted probability and inline equation.
# │ How:     Binomial complement: Pr(Slow) = 1 - (1 - p99)^N_session.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_math, fmt_percent

class TailLatency:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────
    p_fast = 0.99
    n_requests = 100

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────
    p_all_fast = p_fast**n_requests
    p_slow = 1 - p_all_fast

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────
    check(round(p_slow * 100, 1) == 63.4, f"Expected ~63.4% slow probability, got {p_slow * 100:.2f}%")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────
    p_all_fast_str = fmt(p_all_fast, precision=3, commas=False)
    p_slow_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_slow, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    p_slow_pct_value_str = fmt_percent(p_slow, precision=1, commas=False, style='number')
    p_slow_math = fmt_math(f"\\Pr(\\text{{Slow}}) = 1 - ({p_fast})^{{{n_requests}}} " f"\\approx 1 - {p_all_fast_str} = {p_slow_pct_value_str}\\%")
```

::: {#nbk-appendix-data-median-experience .callout-notebook title="The median experience"}

For $\SessionRequestCount= 100$ independent requests, each with a 0.01 chance of being slow, the probability of at least one p99-tail event is `{python} TailLatency.p_slow_math`.

**Systems insight**: With independent requests, a 100-request session is more likely than not to include an event beyond p99. Correlated slowdowns can change this probability [@dean2013].

:::

@Sec-model-serving-tail-latency-5376 develops tail latency for a serving system, where queuing produces the tail and request fan-out amplifies it. Tail probabilities describe one measured distribution. Deciding whether a measured rate is itself trustworthy is a sampling question.

### Sampling and estimation {#sec-appdx-data-foundations-sampling-estimation-5b1e}

Every accuracy, error rate, and conversion rate in this book is measured on a finite sample, so every one of them carries sampling error. The question that decides a release is whether a measured number, or a measured difference, is larger than that error. Four tools answer it: an interval for one rate, the sample size that makes the interval narrow enough, a paired test for two models scored on the same examples, and the traffic an online A/B test needs. Each reduces to a short formula for the number of labeled examples or user sessions an engineer must collect.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: sampling-estimation
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SAMPLING AND ESTIMATION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-appdx-data-foundations-sampling-estimation-5b1e
# │
# │ Goal:    Interval for a rate (ResNet-50 on the ImageNet validation set),
# │          sample size for a rate (KWS detection), McNemar for FP32 vs INT8
# │          ResNet-50, and A/B duration for the ML operations scenario.
# │ Show:    Half-widths in percentage points, counts, chi-square, days.
# │ How:     Normal approximation to the binomial; MLSysIM two-proportion
# │          sample size; validation count and clip length from the registry.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from math import sqrt, ceil
from statistics import NormalDist
from mlsysim import Datasets
from mlsysim.core.units import second, minute, hour, ureg
from mlsysim.physics import calc_two_proportion_sample_size
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_percent, fmt_pp, fmt_time

class SamplingEstimation:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────
    confidence = 0.95
    power = 0.80
    n_val = int(Datasets.ImageNet.validation_examples.magnitude)
    resnet_top1 = 0.76  # scenario assumption: ResNet-50 top-1 as quoted in benchmarking
    n_base_only = 300  # scenario assumption: images only FP32 ResNet-50 gets right
    n_comp_only = 250  # scenario assumption: images only INT8 ResNet-50 gets right
    kws_detect = 0.98  # scenario assumption: KWS detection-rate target from data engineering
    kws_half_pp = 0.5  # scenario assumption: target interval half-width (points)
    clip_duration = Datasets.MSWC.sample_duration
    ab_baseline = 0.05  # scenario assumption: A/B conversion baseline (ML operations scenario)
    ab_rel_lift = 0.02  # scenario assumption: relative lift to detect
    ab_users_per_arm_per_day = 100_000  # scenario assumption: daily users routed to each arm

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────
    z = NormalDist().inv_cdf(1 - (1 - confidence) / 2)
    z_beta = NormalDist().inv_cdf(power)
    ci_half_pp = z * sqrt(resnet_top1 * (1 - resnet_top1) / n_val) * 100
    diff_half_pp = ci_half_pp * sqrt(2)
    net_drop_images = n_base_only - n_comp_only
    net_drop_pp = net_drop_images / n_val * 100
    chi2 = (n_base_only - n_comp_only) ** 2 / (n_base_only + n_comp_only)
    chi2_crit = z**2
    kws_n = ceil(z**2 * kws_detect * (1 - kws_detect) / (kws_half_pp / 100) ** 2)
    kws_n_half = ceil(z**2 * kws_detect * (1 - kws_detect) / (kws_half_pp / 200) ** 2)
    kws_audio_time = kws_n * clip_duration
    kws_audio_half_time = kws_n_half * clip_duration
    ab_n = ceil(calc_two_proportion_sample_size(ab_baseline, ab_baseline * ab_rel_lift, z_alpha=z, z_beta=z_beta))
    ab_days = ab_n / ab_users_per_arm_per_day

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────
    check(0.3 < ci_half_pp < 0.45, f"ImageNet half-width drifted: {ci_half_pp:.3f} pp")
    check(net_drop_pp < diff_half_pp, "The paired example must sit inside the unpaired interval")
    check(chi2 > chi2_crit, "The paired example must resolve the drop")
    check(kws_n_half == 4 * kws_n or abs(kws_n_half - 4 * kws_n) <= 3, "Halving the width must quadruple the sample")
    check(740_000 <= ab_n <= 750_000, f"A/B sample size must match the ML operations scenario, got {ab_n:,}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────
    z_str = fmt(z, precision=2, commas=False)
    confidence_pct_str = fmt_percent(confidence, precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
    power_pct_str = fmt_percent(power, precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
    n_val_str = fmt(n_val, precision=0, commas=True)
    resnet_top1_pct_str = fmt_percent(resnet_top1, precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
    ci_half_pp_str = fmt_pp(ci_half_pp, precision=1, commas=False, style="prose")
    diff_half_pp_str = fmt_pp(diff_half_pp, precision=1, commas=False, style="prose")
    n_base_only_str = fmt(n_base_only, precision=0, commas=False)
    n_comp_only_str = fmt(n_comp_only, precision=0, commas=False)
    net_drop_images_str = fmt(net_drop_images, precision=0, commas=False)
    net_drop_pp_str = fmt_pp(net_drop_pp, precision=1, commas=False, style="prose")
    chi2_str = fmt(chi2, precision=2, commas=False)
    chi2_crit_str = fmt(chi2_crit, precision=2, commas=False)
    kws_detect_pct_str = fmt_percent(kws_detect, precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
    kws_half_pp_str = fmt_pp(kws_half_pp, precision=1, commas=False, style="prose")
    kws_half_half_pp_str = fmt_pp(kws_half_pp / 2, precision=2, commas=False, style="prose")
    kws_n_str = fmt(kws_n, precision=0, commas=True)
    kws_n_half_str = fmt(kws_n_half, precision=0, commas=True)
    kws_audio_min_str = fmt_time(round(kws_audio_time.to(minute)), minute, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    kws_audio_half_h_str = fmt_time(kws_audio_half_time, hour, precision=1, commas=False, style="word")
    ab_baseline_pct_str = fmt_percent(ab_baseline, precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
    ab_rel_lift_pct_str = fmt_percent(ab_rel_lift, precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
    ab_n_str = fmt(ab_n, precision=0, commas=True)
    ab_users_per_arm_per_day_str = fmt(ab_users_per_arm_per_day, precision=0, commas=True)
    ab_days_str = fmt(ab_days, precision=1, commas=False)
```

The first tool is the **confidence interval for a rate**\index{Confidence interval!appendix refresher}. A model that classifies a fraction $\EstimatedAccuracy$ of $\EvaluationSampleCount$ independent examples correctly has, by the normal approximation to the binomial, an interval of

$$ \EstimatedAccuracy \pm \ConfidenceCriticalQuantile \sqrt{\frac{\EstimatedAccuracy(1-\EstimatedAccuracy)}{\EvaluationSampleCount}} $$ {#eq-appdx-data-rate-interval}

at the confidence level $\ConfidenceCriticalQuantile$ encodes (`{python} SamplingEstimation.z_str` for `{python} SamplingEstimation.confidence_pct_str`). ResNet-50 at `{python} SamplingEstimation.resnet_top1_pct_str` top-1 on the `{python} SamplingEstimation.n_val_str`-image ImageNet validation set is therefore known only to within about `{python} SamplingEstimation.ci_half_pp_str`. Two models scored on independent samples of that size have a difference interval about $\sqrt{2}$ times wider, because the variances of the two estimates add, roughly `{python} SamplingEstimation.diff_half_pp_str`. A smaller accuracy gap between them cannot be resolved that way. @Sec-benchmarking-statistical-methodological-issues-7aa5 applies the interval to benchmark reports and shows why a single accuracy number without one is not a result.

When the evaluation set has not yet been collected, solving @eq-appdx-data-rate-interval for $\EvaluationSampleCount$ gives the required **sample size for a rate**\index{Sample size!rate estimation}: the critical value squared, times $\EstimatedAccuracy(1-\EstimatedAccuracy)$, divided by the square of the target half-width. Because the half-width falls only as the square root of the count, halving it quadruples the labeling cost. A keyword spotter expected to detect `{python} SamplingEstimation.kws_detect_pct_str` of wake words needs `{python} SamplingEstimation.kws_n_str` labeled one-second clips to pin that rate within `{python} SamplingEstimation.kws_half_pp_str` (about `{python} SamplingEstimation.kws_audio_min_str` of audio). Reaching `{python} SamplingEstimation.kws_half_half_pp_str` takes `{python} SamplingEstimation.kws_n_half_str` clips (`{python} SamplingEstimation.kws_audio_half_h_str`). The count applies to every slice that must be certified separately. @Sec-responsible-engineering-predeployment-assessment-2324 multiplies it across demographic subgroups, where a rare group must be oversampled to reach the count at all. @Sec-data-selection-computeoptimal-frontier-24ba needs it to confirm that a curated subset still reaches the target accuracy.

When a baseline and a compressed model are scored on the same validation set, **McNemar's test**\index{McNemar's test!appendix refresher} sharpens the comparison because the examples both models get right or both get wrong cancel out. Only the discordant counts matter: $\BaselineOnlyCorrectCount$ examples that only the baseline gets right and $\CompressedOnlyCorrectCount$ that only the compressed model gets right. The test statistic is

$$ \McnemarTestStatistic = \frac{(\BaselineOnlyCorrectCount - \CompressedOnlyCorrectCount)^2}{\BaselineOnlyCorrectCount + \CompressedOnlyCorrectCount}, $$ {#eq-appdx-data-mcnemar}

and the difference is significant at `{python} SamplingEstimation.confidence_pct_str` when it exceeds `{python} SamplingEstimation.chi2_crit_str` (the square of `{python} SamplingEstimation.z_str`). Suppose FP32 and INT8 ResNet-50 disagree on the ImageNet validation set as follows, an illustrative split: `{python} SamplingEstimation.n_base_only_str` images only the FP32 model gets right and `{python} SamplingEstimation.n_comp_only_str` only the INT8 model gets right. The net loss is `{python} SamplingEstimation.net_drop_images_str` images, `{python} SamplingEstimation.net_drop_pp_str` of accuracy, well inside the unpaired interval above, yet @eq-appdx-data-mcnemar gives $\McnemarTestStatistic=$ `{python} SamplingEstimation.chi2_str`, which exceeds the threshold. Pairing resolves a drop that independent samples could not, which is why an evaluation harness must keep per-example outcomes rather than only the two accuracies. @Sec-benchmarking-statistical-methodological-issues-7aa5 works through the case in which the same marginal scores leave the verdict open, and @sec-model-compression produces the INT8 model whose accuracy loss the test checks.

When the comparison moves to live traffic, an online **A/B test**\index{A/B testing!sample size} assigns users at random to a control arm and a treatment arm and compares a rate, such as conversion, between them. Let $\MinimumDetectableEffect$ be the smallest absolute difference worth detecting, $\OutcomeStandardDeviation^2$ the per-user variance (the baseline rate times one minus it for a yes-or-no outcome), and $\PowerCriticalQuantile$ the critical value for the chosen power. The users needed per arm are

$$ \RequiredUsersPerVariant = \frac{2(\ConfidenceCriticalQuantile + \PowerCriticalQuantile)^2 \OutcomeStandardDeviation^2}{\MinimumDetectableEffect^2}. $$ {#eq-appdx-data-ab-sample-size}

For a `{python} SamplingEstimation.ab_rel_lift_pct_str` relative lift on a `{python} SamplingEstimation.ab_baseline_pct_str` baseline at `{python} SamplingEstimation.confidence_pct_str` confidence and `{python} SamplingEstimation.power_pct_str` power, @eq-appdx-data-ab-sample-size requires `{python} SamplingEstimation.ab_n_str` users per arm in the release scenario of @sec-ml-operations-ab-testing-model-validation-e480. A service that can route `{python} SamplingEstimation.ab_users_per_arm_per_day_str` users per day to each arm needs about `{python} SamplingEstimation.ab_days_str` days to finish one test. That duration, not compute, sets how often a recommendation model can be released on evidence.

Each of these tools assumes the examples come from one fixed population. When the population itself moves, the question changes from estimating a rate to detecting that the distribution has shifted.

### Measuring drift {#sec-appdx-data-foundations-measuring-drift-divergence-a6dd}

Comparing means is not enough to catch that shift, because a distribution's tails or bin shares can move while its average stays fixed. Comparing the serving distribution ($\CurrentDistribution$) with the training distribution ($\TrainingDistribution$) therefore requires a distance measure across the full distribution shape: KL divergence and the population stability index for binned features, and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) statistic for continuous ones. @Sec-data-engineering-detecting-responding-data-drift-509a develops drift detection and its taxonomy around these three measures, and @sec-ml-operations-production-monitoring-5e1b decides what an alert should trigger.

For discrete outcomes $\DiscreteOutcome$, @eq-appdx-data-kl-divergence expresses KL divergence\index{Kullback-Leibler divergence!appendix refresher}[^fn-kl-divergence-relative] as the expected extra coding cost of approximating $\CurrentDistribution$ with $\TrainingDistribution$ [@kullback1951; @cover2006]. The displayed form is finite only when $\TrainingDistribution(\DiscreteOutcome) > 0$ wherever $\CurrentDistribution(\DiscreteOutcome) > 0$. Production implementations therefore need explicit smoothing or zero handling.
$$ \KlDivergence(\CurrentDistribution \lVert \TrainingDistribution) = \sum_\DiscreteOutcome\CurrentDistribution(\DiscreteOutcome) \log \frac{\CurrentDistribution(\DiscreteOutcome)}{\TrainingDistribution(\DiscreteOutcome)} $$ {#eq-appdx-data-kl-divergence}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: kl-divergence-drift
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ KL DIVERGENCE DRIFT DETECTION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Callout "Worked Example: KL Divergence for Drift Detection",
# │          @sec-appdx-data-foundations-measuring-drift-divergence-a6dd narrative.
# │
# │ Goal:    Compute KL(P_0 lVert P_t), KL(P_t lVert P_0), and PSI for a worked drift example.
# │ Show:    Step-by-step formulas, intermediate terms, and final values.
# │ How:     Elementwise log-ratios, weighted sums, PSI symmetrization.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, check, fmt_math, MarkdownStr, fmt_percent

class KLDrift:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    P0 = [0.60, 0.30, 0.10]  # scenario assumption: KWS training windows by SNR bin (high, medium, low)
    Pt = [0.45, 0.40, 0.15]  # scenario assumption: fleet windows after the microphone change

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    lr = [math.log(p0 / pt) for p0, pt in zip(P0, Pt)]

    kl_pq_t = [p0 * l for p0, l in zip(P0, lr)]
    kl_pq = sum(kl_pq_t)

    kl_qp_t = [pt * (-l) for pt, l in zip(Pt, lr)]
    kl_qp = sum(kl_qp_t)

    diffs = [p0 - pt for p0, pt in zip(P0, Pt)]
    psi_t = [d * l for d, l in zip(diffs, lr)]
    psi = sum(psi_t)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(kl_pq - 0.0458) < 0.001, f"KL(P_0 lVert P_t) drifted: {kl_pq:.4f}")
    check(abs(kl_qp - 0.0464) < 0.001, f"KL(P_t lVert P_0) drifted: {kl_qp:.4f}")
    check(abs(psi - 0.0922) < 0.001, f"PSI drifted: {psi:.4f}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    # Internal interpolation helpers (no _str suffix — not exported to prose).
    _P0_fmt = [f"{p0:.2f}" for p0 in P0]
    _Pt_fmt = [f"{pt:.2f}" for pt in Pt]
    _lr_fmt = [f"{l:.4f}" for l in lr]

    _kl_pq_t_fmt = [f"{t:.4f}" for t in kl_pq_t]
    _kl_qp_t_fmt = [f"{t:.4f}" for t in kl_qp_t]
    _diff_fmt = [f"{d:.2f}" for d in diffs]
    _psi_t_fmt = [f"{t:.5f}" for t in psi_t]

    # Scalar prose exports
    kl_pq_str = fmt(kl_pq, precision=4, commas=False)
    kl_qp_str = fmt(kl_qp, precision=4, commas=False)
    psi_str = fmt(psi, precision=4, commas=False)
    p0_high_pct_str = fmt_percent(P0[0], precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
    p0_medium_pct_str = fmt_percent(P0[1], precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
    p0_low_pct_str = fmt_percent(P0[2], precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
    pt_high_pct_str = fmt_percent(Pt[0], precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
    pt_medium_pct_str = fmt_percent(Pt[1], precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
    pt_low_pct_str = fmt_percent(Pt[2], precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")

    # Bracketed vectors and display equations are structural math strings.
    P0_vec_str = MarkdownStr(f"[{_P0_fmt[0]}, {_P0_fmt[1]}, {_P0_fmt[2]}]")
    Pt_vec_str = MarkdownStr(f"[{_Pt_fmt[0]}, {_Pt_fmt[1]}, {_Pt_fmt[2]}]")

    # Renamed from kl_pq_formula → kl_pq_eq (canonical _eq suffix for fmt_math expression)
    kl_pq_eq = MarkdownStr(
        "\\begin{gather*}\n"
        f"\\mathcal{{D}}_{{\\text{{KL}}}}(P_0 \\lVert P_t) = {_P0_fmt[0]} \\log\\frac{{{_P0_fmt[0]}}}{{{_Pt_fmt[0]}}} "
        f"+ {_P0_fmt[1]} \\log\\frac{{{_P0_fmt[1]}}}{{{_Pt_fmt[1]}}} "
        f"+ {_P0_fmt[2]} \\log\\frac{{{_P0_fmt[2]}}}{{{_Pt_fmt[2]}}}"
        "\\end{gather*}"
    )
    # Renamed from kl_pq_calc → kl_pq_calc_eq
    kl_pq_calc_eq = MarkdownStr(
        "\\begin{gather*}\n"
        f"= {_P0_fmt[0]} \\times {_lr_fmt[0]} "
        f"+ {_P0_fmt[1]} \\times ({_lr_fmt[1]}) "
        f"+ {_P0_fmt[2]} \\times ({_lr_fmt[2]}) "
        "\\\\[-1pt]\n"
        f"= {_kl_pq_t_fmt[0]} + ({_kl_pq_t_fmt[1]}) + ({_kl_pq_t_fmt[2]}) "
        f"= {kl_pq_str}\\text{{ nats}}"
        "\\end{gather*}"
    )
    # Renamed from kl_qp_formula → kl_qp_eq
    kl_qp_eq = MarkdownStr(
        "\\begin{gather*}\n"
        f"\\mathcal{{D}}_{{\\text{{KL}}}}(P_t \\lVert P_0) = {_Pt_fmt[0]} \\log\\frac{{{_Pt_fmt[0]}}}{{{_P0_fmt[0]}}} "
        f"+ {_Pt_fmt[1]} \\log\\frac{{{_Pt_fmt[1]}}}{{{_P0_fmt[1]}}} "
        f"+ {_Pt_fmt[2]} \\log\\frac{{{_Pt_fmt[2]}}}{{{_P0_fmt[2]}}}"
        "\\end{gather*}"
    )
    # Renamed from kl_qp_calc → kl_qp_calc_eq
    kl_qp_calc_eq = MarkdownStr(
        "\\begin{gather*}\n"
        f"= {_Pt_fmt[0]} \\times ({-lr[0]:.4f}) "
        f"+ {_Pt_fmt[1]} \\times ({-lr[1]:.4f}) "
        f"+ {_Pt_fmt[2]} \\times ({-lr[2]:.4f}) "
        "\\\\[-1pt]\n"
        f"= {_kl_qp_t_fmt[0]} + {_kl_qp_t_fmt[1]} + {_kl_qp_t_fmt[2]} "
        f"= {kl_qp_str}\\text{{ nats}}"
        "\\end{gather*}"
    )
    psi_eq = MarkdownStr(
        "\\begin{gather*}\n"
        f"\\text{{PSI}} = \\sum (P_{{0,i}} - P_{{t,i}}) "
        f"\\log\\frac{{P_{{0,i}}}}{{P_{{t,i}}}} "
        f"= ({_diff_fmt[0]})({_lr_fmt[0]}) "
        f"+ ({_diff_fmt[1]})({_lr_fmt[1]}) "
        f"+ ({_diff_fmt[2]})({_lr_fmt[2]}) "
        "\\\\[-1pt]\n"
        f"= {_psi_t_fmt[0]} + {_psi_t_fmt[1]} + {_psi_t_fmt[2]} "
        f"= {psi_str}\n"
        "\\end{gather*}"
    )

KLDrift.P0_fmt = KLDrift._P0_fmt
KLDrift.Pt_fmt = KLDrift._Pt_fmt
KLDrift.lr_fmt = KLDrift._lr_fmt
KLDrift.kl_pq_t_fmt = KLDrift._kl_pq_t_fmt
KLDrift.kl_qp_t_fmt = KLDrift._kl_qp_t_fmt
KLDrift.diff_fmt = KLDrift._diff_fmt
KLDrift.psi_t_fmt = KLDrift._psi_t_fmt
```

::: {#nbk-appendix-data-kl-divergence-drift-detection .callout-notebook title="Worked example: KL divergence for drift detection"}

**Scenario**: A keyword-spotting model was trained on audio windows binned by signal-to-noise ratio: `{python} KLDrift.p0_high_pct_str` high, `{python} KLDrift.p0_medium_pct_str` medium, and `{python} KLDrift.p0_low_pct_str` low. After the device maker changes the microphone in a new product generation, the windows arriving from the fleet shift to `{python} KLDrift.pt_high_pct_str` high, `{python} KLDrift.pt_medium_pct_str` medium, and `{python} KLDrift.pt_low_pct_str` low.

**Math**:

Training distribution $\TrainingDistribution$: `{python} KLDrift.P0_vec_str`. Serving distribution $\CurrentDistribution$: `{python} KLDrift.Pt_vec_str`.
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(r"\vspace{-4mm}")
print(KLDrift.kl_qp_eq)
print(r"\vspace{-6mm}")
print(KLDrift.kl_qp_calc_eq)
print(r"\vspace{-4mm}")
print(KLDrift.kl_pq_eq)
print(r"\vspace{-6mm}")
print(KLDrift.kl_pq_calc_eq)
```

The two directions give different values, $\KlDivergence(\TrainingDistribution \lVert \CurrentDistribution) \neq \KlDivergence(\CurrentDistribution \lVert \TrainingDistribution)$. The population stability index (PSI)\index{Population stability index!appendix refresher} symmetrizes this by summing the two directions. The calculation below uses natural logarithms:
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(r"\vspace{-4mm}")
print(KLDrift.psi_eq)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: psi-threshold
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: PSI threshold prose in this callout
# │ Goal: PSI warning (0.1) and critical (0.25) thresholds, matching the
# │       bands used in the data engineering and ML operations chapters.
# │ Show: Both thresholds as prose-local scalars.
# │ How: Load the monitoring thresholds from MLSysIM and guard the expected values.
from mlsysim import Ops
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, check

class PsiThreshold:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    psi_threshold = Ops.Monitoring.PsiWarnThreshold
    psi_critical = Ops.Monitoring.PsiCriticalThreshold
    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(psi_threshold - 0.1) < 1e-12, f"Expected PSI warning threshold 0.1, got {psi_threshold}")
    check(abs(psi_critical - 0.25) < 1e-12, f"Expected PSI critical threshold 0.25, got {psi_critical}")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    psi_threshold_str = fmt(psi_threshold, precision=1, commas=False)
    psi_critical_str = fmt(psi_critical, precision=2, commas=False)
```

**Systems insight**: Since PSI = `{python} KLDrift.psi_str` < `{python} PsiThreshold.psi_threshold_str`, this drift sits just below the conventional warning threshold and well short of the critical threshold of `{python} PsiThreshold.psi_critical_str` used in @sec-ml-operations. The right response is to keep the feature on the monitoring dashboard and look for corroborating drift signals rather than retraining from this statistic alone. The statistic is also cheap to collect on an always-on device, which can report three bin counters per interval instead of raw audio, so the check fits the power budget and raw recordings never need to leave the device.

:::

[^fn-kl-divergence-relative]: **KL divergence**\index{Kullback-Leibler divergence!appendix refresher}: Named after Solomon Kullback\index{Kullback, Solomon|seealso{Kullback-Leibler divergence}} and Richard Leibler\index{Leibler, Richard|seealso{Kullback-Leibler divergence}}, who introduced it in 1951. Also called *relative entropy*, it quantifies the expected extra information needed to encode samples from one distribution using a code optimized for another; for drift monitoring in this book, the canonical direction is $\KlDivergence(\CurrentDistribution \lVert \TrainingDistribution)$. With natural logarithms, as in the example above, the unit is nats; with base-2 logarithms, the unit is bits.

Those PSI thresholds remain illustrative because their meaning depends on sample size, binning, smoothing, and zero handling, and because retraining requires model-quality evidence. Moreover, KL divergence and PSI compare binned or categorical distributions. For a continuous feature, such as the loudness of an audio window, the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic\index{Kolmogorov-Smirnov test!appendix refresher} avoids binning altogether. It is the largest gap between the empirical cumulative distribution functions of a training sample and a serving sample,

$$\KolmogorovSmirnovStatistic= \max_{\MonitoredFeatureLevel}|\TrainingEmpiricalCdf(\MonitoredFeatureLevel) - \ServingEmpiricalCdf(\MonitoredFeatureLevel)|.$$

Its critical value shrinks with the square root of the sample sizes, so a large serving sample flags even a tiny shift as significant. Whether that shift matters is a separate question. @Sec-data-engineering-quality-validation-monitoring-498f works the test through with its critical value. All three measures rest on information theory\index{Information theory}, which supplies their units.

### Information theory for systems {#sec-appdx-data-foundations-information-theory-systems-c033}

A training run can consume more examples, run longer, and still stop improving if the added data carries too little useful signal. At that point the limit is the information the data pipeline delivers to the learner, not compute or bandwidth. @Sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-information-roofline-destination-6426 treats that data quality limit as a diagnostic constraint, and information theory provides the units for reasoning about it.

* **Entropy ($\ShannonEntropy$)**\index{Entropy!definition}:[^fn-entropy-information-theory] The average uncertainty in a distribution, defined as $\ShannonEntropy(\DiscreteRandomVariable) = -\sum \ProbabilityFunction(\DiscreteOutcome) \log \ProbabilityFunction(\DiscreteOutcome)$. The log base sets the unit: natural logs give nats, while $\log_2$ gives bits. A uniform distribution has maximum entropy only over a fixed finite support. This connects directly to KL divergence above: $\KlDivergence$ measures the excess coding cost of using the wrong distribution.
* **Information density**\index{Information density!definition}: Used here as a book-level heuristic for useful learning signal per unit of storage, not as a standard information-theory quantity.
* **Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)**\index{Signal-to-noise ratio!definition}: The ratio of signal power to noise power. In ML, the book uses low SNR qualitatively for data in which task-relevant structure is weak relative to noise; adding compute cannot compensate for missing task-relevant signal.

[^fn-entropy-information-theory]: **Entropy**\index{Entropy!appendix refresher}: Shannon\index{Shannon, Claude!information theory} adopted the term in 1948 to quantify information content [@shannon1948]. In systems terms, Shannon entropy is a lower bound on average lossless code length. Practical prefix codes approach it, and block codes can approach it asymptotically. These bounds inform compression ratios and data-pipeline sizing.

Together with tail probabilities, finite-sample intervals, and drift divergences, these quantities complete the statistical half of the data foundations: the first half of the appendix prices how fast bytes move and decode, and the second prices how much evidence those bytes actually carry.
